source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Closest direct use of ACH inside an LLM loop. A decider agent gets a fixed ACH protocol: list exclusive hypotheses, pool all evidence first, fill a hypothesis-by-evidence matrix (consistent/inconsistent/irrelevant), then a bias-review step.
numbers: Benchmarks MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-Challenge. Agents: GLM-4-9B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-2-72B, GPT-4. Decider trained from Qwen-7B-Base with GRPO (5 rollouts per prompt, temp 0.6).
limits: Only multiple-choice QA, not intelligence problems. ACH here is a scaffold on aggregation, not on analysts' evidence.
agent_relevance: ACH matrix is a usable aggregation step for our agent: hypothesis list, shared evidence pool, per-cell verdict, review pass.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Zero-shot ACH prompting alone (no training) beat an unstructured decider and all seven voting rules.
numbers: Homogeneous ACH beat Informed Dictatorial by 1.9 points on All Average and beat all voting methods. All Average: single agent 66.0; voting rules 79.9 to 80.6; informed dictatorial 82.9 (+2.3); ACH with Qwen-7B-Instruct 82.2 (+1.6); ACH with Qwen-7B-R1 87.6 (+7.0); trained AgentCDM 88.4 (+7.8).
quote: systematic, evidence-driven evaluation of competing hypotheses is, in itself, an effective approach
limits: Gain from prompt-only ACH is small (about 2 points). Most of the gain needs RL training. Table row alignment was read from a text extract; check against the PDF before reuse.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot ACH helps a little; do not expect large gains from the prompt alone. Keep a plain judge as control.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Ablation: scaffolding alone hurt; exploration alone did not help; both together won. A fixed ACH scaffold made the model rigid.
numbers: Accuracy Full / Vanilla prompt / Scaffolding-only / Exploration-only: MMLU 78.5/72.6/68.1/71.5; MMLU-Pro 65.2/52.5/49.4/52.1; ARC-C 96.0/89.0/84.0/89.7.
limits: Trained model, so not a pure prompt result. Single run, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Rigid use of a fixed matrix every time can be worse than no scaffold (49.4 vs 52.5 on MMLU-Pro). Fits our rule: apply on a signal, not always.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: ACH decider gains depend on agent quality: more agents helped GPT-4 but hurt weak models. With mixed pools the trained decider beat zero-shot ACH.
numbers: Heterogeneous pool, MMLU-Pro: AgentCDM 67.9 vs Qwen-7B-Instruct with ACH 55.9. Mistral-7B got worse as agent count rose. Gains over single agent on MMLU-Pro: +22.5 (Llama-3), +29.3 (Mistral-7B).
limits: Authors' reason (noise amplified by weak inputs) is not tested.
agent_relevance: Adding more weak voters is not safe. Matches our rule that same-model samples are not independent.

source: Evron (2026) Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
finding: Scales ACH from a few hypotheses to thousands: each hypothesis is a machine-checkable brain scored against every new observation. Contradiction lowers standing; absence does not.
numbers: Synthetic tests only: 6,000 host-days per test; one-link SUNBURST brain fired on 594 of 6,000; behavioral brain fired in 100 of 100 rotated-indicator runs while the indicator twin fired on the first run only; Discover found the planted pattern in 30 of 30 runs but proposed about 25 benign patterns per run.
limits: Author says tests give no detection rate. Disproof is not built. Real pieces co-occur, so separation tests are optimistic. 25 brains from public reports: of 47 verdicts, 23 judged; 9 persisted, 4 replaced.
agent_relevance: Shows ACH can be coded: weights by rarity (negative log2 of base rate) are computed by code, not by the model. Matches G5.

source: Evron (2026) Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
finding: LLM use is fenced by code rules: the model sees only pieces that matched deterministically with rarity scores; evidence naming none is discarded; confidence is capped at 0.4 unless a piece has rarity 0.5 or more.
numbers: Cap 0.4, rarity threshold 0.5. Extraction drops technique IDs outside a curated ATT&CK subset.
quote: Confidence is capped at 0.4 unless one of these pieces has a rarity of 0.5 or more.
limits: Thresholds are design choices, not tuned on real data. Tests of these rules use recorded model output, no live model.
agent_relevance: A concrete template for a code-checked ACH step: the model gives a verdict only inside a frame the program builds, and a cap stops confident claims on weak evidence.

source: Evron (2026) Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
finding: Design rule: a brain's own conclusions never re-enter as new evidence; status (test, active) stays visible so a weighted guess does not look like a fact.
numbers: Design rule only; not measured.
limits: No experiment on whether this prevents circular support.
agent_relevance: Same as our guardrail against self-confirming evidence: derived claims do not count as evidence.

source: Vink et al. (2026) GroundWork: Bridging Human and LLM Reasoning Through a Structured Argumentation Model
finding: Mixed human-LLM tool with an ACH-style evidence-by-claim matrix: the LLM assigns each evidence item a stance (support, attack, neutral) toward two or more competing claims; neutral items are hidden.
numbers: Expert study N=4 (consulting, product, law, immunology); three scenarios. Intelligence scenario: two opposed five-year claims on US rare-earth magnet supply, 5 public reports; neither claim well supported because most evidence fit both.
limits: N=4 interviews, thematic analysis, no accuracy measure. LLM stance accuracy not reported in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Shows the ACH point that shared evidence does not discriminate, and that the matrix exposes it. Useful display for a diagnosticity check.

source: Vink et al. (2026) GroundWork: Bridging Human and LLM Reasoning Through a Structured Argumentation Model
finding: Experts said a persistent, editable argument state beat chat.
numbers: Four experts; one said a chat is static, whereas GroundWork is dynamic.
quote: a chat is static, whereas GroundWork is dynamic
limits: Small sample from authors' networks.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping hypotheses and evidence as explicit program state, not chat history.

source: Gefen et al. (2026) Optimize the Harness, Not the Model (CLEO), CIKM 2026
finding: Government intelligence-analyst agent. A minimal 3k-line harness around a fixed open model (GLM-5.1) nearly matched a 512k-line Claude Code SDK baseline on 240 held-out investigative questions with misleading and contradictory evidence.
numbers: Pass rate: Claude Code SDK bare 85.0% (512k LOC), PI #1 bare 80.8% (75k LOC), PI #2 with CLEO prompts 83.8% (75k), CLEO 83.8% (3k LOC). 300+ expert questions, 240 held out, 3 use cases, about 8,000 files each.
limits: Three-page paper; LLM judge; own datasets; no SAT such as ACH or devil's advocacy tested.
agent_relevance: A small justified scaffold matched a big one. Their justification gate (generic, auditable, lean) mirrors our section 4b.

source: Gefen et al. (2026) Optimize the Harness, Not the Model (CLEO), CIKM 2026
finding: Bottom-up harness growth matched top-down pruning on accuracy but gave a far smaller harness. A cite() helper aimed at the judge's complaint about missing evidence was reverted because the agent rarely used it.
numbers: Top-down matched bottom-up on accuracy but barely shrank the harness; adoption gate evaluated on 32 fixed plus 12 random Q&A per round.
limits: No numbers for the top-down arm in the pages read.
agent_relevance: Add scaffold parts only when an eval shows a need; drop parts the model ignores.

source: Jin and Shin (2026) ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
finding: Cyber threat-intelligence extraction: role-specialised LLM experts propose, then each candidate is verified in a bipolar argumentation graph. Single-pass frontier models had higher recall but low precision.
numbers: TRAM2: GPT-5.5 recall 0.561 but precision 0.335, vs sentence-level NER precision 0.654. ARBITRA F1 0.649, 15.5 points above the strongest TTPrint setup. Under adversarial perturbations its precision loss is about half that of frontier baselines. Reasoning fine-tune adds 10.3 F1 points vs 4.2 for basic fine-tune.
limits: Cyber-domain labels, not analyst judgments; fine-tuned experts.
agent_relevance: Checking each candidate against its own evidence raises precision. Precision-first design suits cases where a false claim is costly.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Debate (several instances propose, read each other, revise) beat single answer and self-reflection on facts.
numbers: ChatGPT. Biographies 73.8 +/-2.3 debate vs 66.0 single vs 68.3 reflection; MMLU 71.1 +/-4.6 vs 63.9 vs 57.7 (reflection hurt); Chess move validity 45.2 vs 29.3 vs 38.8. Personas on MMLU: 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Same base model in all agents; later work could not confirm a lead over self-consistency (see Smit).
agent_relevance: Debate resembles devil's advocacy. Reflection alone hurt on MMLU: another reason to avoid self-critique without a signal.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs (ICML)
finding: Failed to confirm debate's edge: debate protocols did not reliably beat self-consistency or Medprompt ensembling at equal or lower cost.
numbers: Datasets MedQA, PubMedQA, MMLU, CIAR, GPQA, CosmosQA, Chess; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mixtral 8x7B. Prompting 'agree X% of the time' raised Multi-Persona by 15% and Society of Mind by 5% on a 376-question USMLE subset; ChatEval barely changed. Best agreement 90% on MedQA.
limits: Tuned settings did not transfer well to Mixtral. Best agreement differs by dataset: MedQA and PubMedQA liked high agreement; CIAR (counterintuitive) liked disagreement.
agent_relevance: Devil's-advocate strength is a dial with a task-dependent optimum: more dissent helps counterintuitive tasks and hurts routine ones. Do not turn it on by default.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate can lower accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Models flip from correct to incorrect to agree with peers.
numbers: Tasks MMLU, CommonSenseQA, GSM8K; models include Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-4o-mini. Correct-to-incorrect flips are most likely when an agent is alone in its answer and fall as more peers agree. A correctness-payoff prompt did not cut harmful flips.
quote: favoring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning
limits: Exact accuracy deltas are in figures not transcribed. Small models.
agent_relevance: LLM version of conformity; it undercuts voting and conflict-based gains. Needs code-side checks (G4, G5).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Self-critique without outside feedback lowered accuracy. Earlier gains came from oracle labels telling the model when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 standard, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 then 41.8; with oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 to 25.0.
limits: Reasoning tasks; 200-question samples for models other than GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Self-applied devil's advocate (critique your own answer) is not a safe SAT proxy. Revise only from a real failing output (G2).

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: LLMs show human-like biases (anchoring, framing, primacy, group attribution). Mitigation prompts were mixed; having the model rewrite its own prompt (self-help) worked best overall.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2 models. Llama models changed 40 to 52% of decisions between sequential anchor settings. Self-help cut biased framing prompts to 17.2% and status quo to 8.5%. Counterfactual examples sometimes caused complete failure.
limits: Admission-style decision tasks; awareness prompts gave small gains; few-shot sometimes made things worse.
agent_relevance: Be-aware-of-bias prompts give small gains. Debiasing the input works better than adding critique after.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Bigger models gained more from self-help debiasing.
numbers: GPT-4 rewrote prompts to remove bias better than GPT-3.5-turbo.
limits: Capacity effect from few models.
agent_relevance: Scaffold gains depend on model size; test on our actual model.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Self-reflection suffers Degeneration of Thought: once confident, the model stops generating new ideas. A debate with affirmative and negative debaters plus a judge fixed some of this.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic accuracy: GPT-4 51.0; GPT-3.5 26.0; +CoT 28.0; +Self-Consistency 29.5; +Self-Reflect 27.5; +MAD 37.0.
limits: Two tasks; the judge is a model; modest tit-for-tat needed; later benchmarks (Smit) do not confirm a general lead.
agent_relevance: Assigned opposing roles can break lock-in when the first answer is wrong; a case for devil's advocacy on hard, counterintuitive items only.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: The agent asks what could go wrong with an action and what the backup is before each step. A devil's-advocate move used inside an agent loop.
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks), GPT-4: success 23.5% after 7 episodes vs LATS 22.7%; plan revisions down 45%; first-trial actions 6.39 vs 4.01 for Plan+Act.
limits: Gain over best baseline under 1 point (23.5 vs 22.7). One benchmark, zero-shot, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Cheap pre-action failure check helps modestly and cuts rework. Fits a pre-mortem at set points.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Five AI assistants showed sycophancy across four free-form tasks; humans and preference models sometimes preferred convincingly written sycophantic answers over correct ones.
numbers: Five assistants, four tasks; effect is a non-negligible fraction of the time (exact rates not transcribed).
limits: Training-origin claim is correlational with preference data.
agent_relevance: Any critic or devil's-advocate model leans toward the stated answer; give it no proposed answer (G5).

source: Jhang (2026) Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
finding: Tests how far LLM probabilities move on one new piece of evidence. Source-reported wording lowers the move slightly; five weighted estimates cut extreme values but also cut evidence sensitivity in small models.
numbers: Seven configurations; 240 pairs for Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, 120 pairs for harnessed ones. Stated direct update moved 18 to 28 points. Reporting lowered it by 2 to 5 points (significant in 6 of 7). Five weighted estimates cut movement by 43% and 68% in the two local models; harnessed change -3.7 to +0.5 points.
limits: Direction-only labels, so no claim about right size. Hypotheses fixed but not publicly registered.
agent_relevance: Weighing evidence is the step that matters in the human reviews; models move the right way but the source-credibility effect is weak. Test elicitation format for sensitivity separately.

source: Jhang (2026) Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
finding: Related work is thin: defeasible NLI checks direction only; ProbCOPA finds models rarely give mid-range values; EvolveCast tests forecast updating with uncontrolled news direction.
numbers: Cites delta-SNLI (Rudinger 2020), ProbCOPA (Kamath 2026), EvolveCast (Yuan 2025).
limits: As described by the authors; those papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: No controlled LLM test of weighing versus seeking evidence on analyst tasks was found.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Cross-dataset transfer: a decider trained on the harder MMLU-Pro generalised to unseen sets; one trained on easy ARC-Challenge transferred poorly to MMLU-Pro.
numbers: Trained on MMLU-Pro: 80.84 on MMLU and 94.0 on ARC-Challenge (as stated in text).
limits: Transfer table not fully read.
agent_relevance: Structured-reasoning habits learned on hard items carry over; easy practice data does not. Relevant if we ever tune scaffold prompts on a dev set: use hard items.

source: Jin and Shin (2026) ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
finding: Threat model mimics deception: conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination, semantic poisoning, grounded in the Olympic Destroyer false-flag case.
numbers: Three adversarial variants of the TRAM2 split; ARBITRA limits mean precision drop to about half that of frontier baselines.
limits: Perturbations written by a teacher model, not real adversaries.
agent_relevance: Deception tests are the right stress for ACH-style checks; build a test set of planted contradictory evidence.

source: Search gap note, this run
finding: arXiv abstract search for structured analytic techniques returned no results; analysis of competing hypotheses returned 4 (AgentCDM, Adversary Brains, a Havana Syndrome essay, a fraud code-word paper). Web search, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were blocked by budget or rate limits.
numbers: 4 arXiv hits for ACH; 0 for SAT. Fraud paper 2103.09606 uses ACH (not opened).
limits: Not exhaustive: arXiv only, no think-tank, RAND or journal sources reached.
agent_relevance: Lack of controlled LLM tests of premortem, key assumptions check, red team on analyst tasks is an open gap. Our own test would be new.
